catalog_quote: Stress typically falls on the penultimate syllable in Biage. In Mountain Koiali, Garland and Garland state that stress is non-contrastive and always falls on the penultimate syllable with the exception of five syllable words, where the stress falls on both the second and fourth syllables (1971:15–16). He also says, “The stressed syllable is usually slightly lengthened and the final syllable is slightly shortened. Otherwise, each syllable, ie. each vowel, tends to exercise its full value” (1971:15). Retsema did not find anything in his analysis of the Biage wordlists that would contradict Garland’s rules if they are applied to Biage as well.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is regularly penultimate; the surveyors add that the Biage wordlist data are consistent with Garland & Garland's (1971) non-contrastive Mountain Koiali pattern (which for 5-syllable words puts stresses on the 2nd and 4th syllables). Note the survey's paraphrase of Garland compresses the Mt Koiali rule (Garland 1971 actually gives initial stress in disyllables, second-syllable stress in 3- and 4-syllable words), so the first-hand Biage claim to retain is 'typically penultimate', hedged by 'typically'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing stated for Biage itself; only the borrowed Mt Koiali remark that five-syllable words carry stress on both the second and fourth syllables.
new_statements.exceptions: None listed; 'typically' implies unlisted exceptions. No claim that stress is contrastive; no minimal pairs.
new_statements.domain_note: Based on isolated citation forms from 190-item SIL-PNG survey wordlists (170 words + 20 phrases) elicited in seven Biage villages in Oct 2006 by Thom Retsema; word-level impressionistic observation in a sociolinguistic survey report, not a phonological analysis.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Biage [bdf], glottocode biag1234, as surveyed in Kanga, Savaea, Kovelo, Ebea, Pelai, Alola and Isurava villages (Oro Province, west of Kokoda) in 2006; this is the variety Dutton (1969) called the Northern Dialect of Mountain Koiari and which ISO 639-3 split from Mountain Koiali [kpx] (moun1252) in 2010 (change request 2009-041). The comparison statements quoted from Garland & Garland 1971 concern Mountain Koiali of Efogi (moun1252), not Biage.

sources.citation: Garland, Roger & Susan Garland. 1971. Mt. Koiali phonemics. Unpublished ms., 22 pp. SIL, Ukarumpa (SIL archive entry 31239).
sources.note: Describes Mountain Koiali (Efogi, Central Province), not Biage: stress non-contrastive and predictable (sec 5.3.2, ms pp.15-16). It is the comparison source the 2015 survey cites; relevant only as the sister-language baseline.

sources.citation: Dutton, T.E. 1969. The peopling of Central Papua: some preliminary observations. Pacific Linguistics B-9. Canberra: ANU.
sources.note: Treats Biage as part of the Northern Dialect of Mountain Koiari (no Biage-specific phonology). General Koiarian section: vocoid glides and 'the interpretation of stress' in Koita, Mountain Koiari and Barai 'needs further investigation'; stress found phonemic in Koiari, Aomie, Managalasi. No placement rule for Mountain Koiari/Biage.
